subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A voltaic (galvanic) cell converts:
questions.explain: A voltaic cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to generate an electric current.

questions.q: In any electrochemical cell, oxidation always occurs at the:
questions.explain: Oxidation occurs at the anode; reduction occurs at the cathode (in both voltaic and electrolytic cells).

questions.q: In any electrochemical cell, reduction always occurs at the:
questions.explain: Reduction (gain of electrons) takes place at the cathode.

questions.q: In a voltaic cell, the anode is the:
questions.explain: In a voltaic cell the anode (oxidation) is negative and the cathode (reduction) is positive.

questions.q: The purpose of the salt bridge in a voltaic cell is to:
options: Complete the circuit and maintain electrical neutrality
questions.explain: Ions flow through the salt bridge to balance charge as the reaction proceeds.

questions.q: An electrolytic cell differs from a voltaic cell because it:
options: Uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction
questions.explain: Electrolysis forces a non-spontaneous redox reaction using an external power supply.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, sodium is produced at the:
questions.explain: Na+ ions are reduced to sodium at the negative cathode; chlorine forms at the anode.

questions.q: During electrolysis of molten NaCl, the product at the anode is:
questions.explain: Cl- ions are oxidised to chlorine gas at the positive anode.

questions.q: In an electrolytic cell, the anode is connected to the:
options: Positive terminal of the power supply
questions.explain: In electrolysis the anode is positive (opposite to a voltaic cell).

questions.q: The standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a standard electrode potential of:
questions.explain: All standard electrode potentials are measured relative to the SHE, defined as 0.00 V.

questions.q: The standard cell potential is calculated as:
questions.explain: Using standard reduction potentials, E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode).

questions.q: A positive standard cell potential indicates that the cell reaction is:
questions.explain: A positive E(cell) corresponds to a negative ΔG, so the reaction is spontaneous.

questions.q: In a Zn/Cu voltaic cell, electrons flow through the external wire from:
questions.explain: Zinc (more reactive) is oxidised at the anode and electrons flow to the copper cathode.

questions.q: During electrolysis, cations migrate towards the:
questions.explain: Positive cations are attracted to the negative cathode, where they are reduced.

questions.q: Electrolysis is used industrially to:
options: Extract reactive metals such as aluminium
questions.explain: Reactive metals are obtained by electrolysis (e.g. aluminium from molten alumina).

questions.q: The greater the difference between the electrode potentials of two half-cells, the:
questions.explain: A bigger gap in reduction potentials gives a larger E(cell).

questions.q: A half-cell with a more positive standard reduction potential will act as the:
questions.explain: The more easily reduced half-cell (more positive E) is the cathode.

questions.q: In a rechargeable battery being recharged, it operates as:
questions.explain: During charging, external electrical energy drives the reverse (non-spontaneous) reaction.

questions.q: During electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride, hydrogen is usually produced at the cathode rather than sodium because:
options: Water/H+ is more easily reduced than Na+
questions.explain: In aqueous solution, hydrogen is preferentially discharged over the very reactive sodium ion.

questions.q: Electron flow in the external circuit of any cell is always from:
questions.explain: Electrons released by oxidation at the anode travel through the wire to the cathode.
